title: Davenport's Inequality as a Mason–Stothers Corollary
content: The header lays out the target — Davenport's inequality $\deg(f^3 - g^2) \ge \tfrac12\deg f + 1$ for coprime non-constant polynomials over a characteristic-zero field — and the strategy: apply the parent entry's `mason_stothers_charZero` to the additive triple $a = f^3$, $b = -g^2$, $c = f^3 - g^2$. The two imports are `Mathlib` (radical machinery, degree lemmas, `omega`) and `Proofs.MasonStothersOQ01`, the parent supplying the characteristic-zero Mason–Stothers bound. The sketch already isolates the two ingredients combined at the end: two *lower* bounds on $\deg\mathrm{rad}(abc)$ from the cube and square, and one hypothesis-free *upper* bound on the radical degree.
mathContext: Mason–Stothers (function-field abc): for coprime $a+b=c$, not all derivatives zero, $\max\{\deg a, \deg b, \deg c\} + 1 \le \deg\mathrm{rad}(abc)$. Davenport is the special case $(a,b,c) = (f^3, -g^2, f^3-g^2)$.

title: Ambient Setting: a Field of Coefficients
content: The development works over an arbitrary field `k` with decidable equality. `DecidableEq k` is a technical convenience for the radical/factorization machinery; the genuine mathematical hypothesis `CharZero k` is attached locally to the theorems that need it (Davenport can fail in characteristic $p$). Opening `Polynomial`, `UniqueFactorizationMonoid`, and `UniqueFactorizationDomain` brings the `radical`, `radical_pow`, `radical_mul_dvd` API into scope unqualified — the radical is defined via the UFD structure of $k[X]$.
mathContext: $k[X]$ is a unique factorization domain; the radical $\mathrm{rad}(p) = \prod_{q \mid p,\, q \text{ irreducible}} q$ is the squarefree part, so $\deg\mathrm{rad}(p)$ counts the *distinct* roots (with multiplicity one).

title: radical_cube_sq_mul_dvd: The Hypothesis-Free Radical Bound
content: The key combinatorial lemma: $\mathrm{rad}(f^3 g^2 c) \mid f g c$, with **no coprimality hypothesis**. The radical is insensitive to exponents — `radical_pow` gives $\mathrm{rad}(f^3) = \mathrm{rad}(f)$ and $\mathrm{rad}(g^2) = \mathrm{rad}(g)$ — and `radical_mul_dvd` splits a product radical unconditionally. The `calc` chains $\mathrm{rad}(f^3 g^2) \mid \mathrm{rad}(f^3)\mathrm{rad}(g^2) = \mathrm{rad}(f)\mathrm{rad}(g) \mid fg$, then absorbs the $c$ factor with one more `radical_mul_dvd` and `radical_dvd_self`. This is what makes the cube and square contribute only $\deg f$ and $\deg g$ (not $3\deg f$, $2\deg g$) to the distinct-root count.
mathContext: $\mathrm{rad}(f^3 g^2 c) \mid f g c \Rightarrow \deg\mathrm{rad}(f^3 g^2 c) \le \deg f + \deg g + \deg c.$ Divisibility-only result: works even when $f, g$ share roots.

title: Davenport: Building the Coprime Additive Triple
content:
The main theorem opens by assembling the Mason–Stothers inputs for $(a,b,c) = (f^3, -g^2, f^3-g^2)$. Non-vanishing of all three terms follows from $f

e 0$). Coprimality $f^3 \perp -g^2$ comes from `(hcop.pow).neg_right` — coprimality is preserved under taking powers and negation. The additive relation $f^3 + (-g^2) = f^3 - g^2$ is `ring`. The non-triviality disjunct (needed so Mason–Stothers does not degenerate) is supplied by $\deg(f^3) = 3\deg f

mathContext: `IsCoprime f g` ⟹ `IsCoprime (f^3) (-g^2)` via `IsCoprime.pow` then `neg_right`. The triple must be coprime and additive ($a+b=c$) for Mason–Stothers to apply.

title: Applying Mason–Stothers and Normalising the Radical
content: Invoking the parent's `mason_stothers_charZero` yields two lower bounds `b1`, `b2` on $\deg\mathrm{rad}(f^3\cdot(-g^2)\cdot c)$ — one from the $f^3$ term, one from the $g^2$ term. Since $f^3(-g^2)c = -(f^3 g^2 c)$ differs from $f^3 g^2 c$ only by the unit $-1$, `radical_neg` identifies their radicals, letting the hypothesis-free upper bound (in terms of $f^3 g^2 c$) apply. `natDegree_le_of_dvd` combined with `radical_cube_sq_mul_dvd` and `natDegree_mul` then gives the upper bound $\deg\mathrm{rad} \le \deg f + \deg g + \deg c$.
mathContext: $\mathrm{rad}(f^3(-g^2)c) = \mathrm{rad}(-(f^3 g^2 c)) = \mathrm{rad}(f^3 g^2 c)$ since the radical is unit-invariant. Lower bounds: $3\deg f + 1 \le R$ and $2\deg g + 1 \le R$ where $R = \deg\mathrm{rad}$.

title: The Final Sandwich: omega Closes Davenport
content: With $\deg(f^3) = 3\deg f$ and $\deg(-g^2) = 2\deg g$ substituted into the two lower bounds, the proof feeds everything to `omega`: from $3F + 1 \le R$ and $2G + 1 \le R$ together with $R \le F + G + C$, adding the two lower bounds and using $2R \le 2(F+G+C)$ cancels the $G$ terms to give $F + 2 \le 2C$. This is exactly Davenport's inequality $\deg f + 2 \le 2\deg(f^3 - g^2)$ — a pure linear-arithmetic consequence once the degree facts are in place.

title: Height Form: deg(f³ − g²) ≥ ½ deg f + 1
content: `natDegree_cube_sub_sq_ge` restates Davenport directly as a lower bound on the degree of $f^3 - g^2$, rendered over $\mathbb{N}$ as $\lfloor\deg f / 2\rfloor + 1 \le \deg(f^3 - g^2)$. It is a one-line `omega` corollary of `davenport`. This is the form in which Davenport's inequality is usually quoted — the polynomial shadow of Hall's conjecture, which asks how small $|x^3 - y^2|$ can be for integers, and which (unlike this polynomial statement) remains open.
mathContext: $\deg(f^3 - g^2) \ge \tfrac12\deg f + 1$, i.e. $\lfloor \deg f/2 \rfloor + 1 \le \deg(f^3 - g^2)$ over $\mathbb{N}$. Sharp: equality is attained by the classical Davenport pairs (related to Belyi maps).
